job_33e35f869fde3abc: Postdoctoral Scholar in Physical Oceanography 4D-Var Modeling Position Overview School / Campus / College: College of the Environment Organization: Applied Physics Lab Title: Postdoctoral Scholar in Physical Oceanography 4D-Var Modeling Position Details Position Description The Applied Physics Laboratory at the University of Washington (APL-UW) invites applications for a Postdoctoral Scholar in physical oceanography focused on numerical ocean modeling, ocean data assimilation, and computational methods for understanding and predicting regional and coastal ocean circulation. This is a full-time position for 2 years, with the possibility of a 3rd year renewal. The successful candidate will contribute to the Expeditionary Autonomous Sensing for Tactical Oceanography (EASTO) project, which combines fundamental research on ocean processes and four-dimensional variational (4D-Var) modeling with research involving sensors and autonomous vehicles. The work will address autonomy and path planning; use Observing System Simulation Experiments (OSSEs) to evaluate observing and assimilation strategies; support field experiments; and translate research results into operational path-planning applications. Research is expected to support U.S. Navy and other federal sponsors and collaborators conducting basic and applied oceanographic research. Working under the guidance of Harper Simmons, Senior Principal Oceanographer in APL-UW’s Ocean Physics Department (OPD), the Postdoctoral Scholar will develop, execute, evaluate, and analyze numerical ocean models and data assimilation systems. The scholar will collaborate with scientists and engineers to integrate models and observations, communicate research results, and develop increasing scientific independence. Specific research activities will include: Develop and apply 4D-Var ocean data assimilation and conduct fundamental research on regional and coastal ocean processes using numerical experiments and observations. Design and analyze Observing System Simulation Experiments (OSSEs) to assess observing strategies and the sensitivity of 4D-Var performance to assimilation windows, error models, boundary conditions, and observational coverage. Integrate model estimates and forecasts with observations from oceanographic sensors and autonomous vehicles, and contribute to autonomy and path-planning activities, including fieldwork support and operational path planning. Configure, execute, evaluate, and maintain regional ocean models and data assimilation systems on Unix/Linux and high-performance computing platforms. Evaluate model and assimilation performance using statistical and dynamical diagnostics and verification against independent observations and diagnose performance issues. Develop and maintain scientific software for modeling, assimilation, analysis, visualization, and reproducible computational workflows. Collaborate across disciplines and contribute to documentation, sponsor reports, presentations, peer-reviewed publications, and research proposals. Develop research questions and directions that build on the scholar's interests and advance professional skills and research independence. The Postdoctoral Scholar will work under the direction of principal investigators for the benefit of the research programs, the unit's educational program, and their own professional growth. The Postdoctoral Scholar will be engaged full-time in mentored advanced training to enhance professional skills and research independence. OI is a nonpartisan research and policy institute focused on improving economic opportunity. OI has published seminal work on national trends in upward mobility; racial disparities; the role of neighborhoods, social capital, credit, and higher education in upward mobility; and the use of private-sector data to understand disparate impacts in the recent economic recession and recovery. Much of the team’s ongoing research uses quasi-experimental methods to identify causal effects and test the predictions of economic and sociological models. Examples of current research projects include: long-term impacts of neighborhoods and place-based policies, the role of colleges and workforce training in upward mobility, and measuring how social networks affect mobility. OI’s work has shaped policy discussions at the national and local level, with nearly a dozen of its studies covered on the front pages of major media outlets, such as the New York Times, The Economist, The Washington Post, and the Wall Street Journal, and have been widely cited in policy discussions. In addition to working with OI faculty, predoctoral fellows frequently co-author papers with other students or faculty members. Fellows will interact regularly with professors and their collaborators – such as Stefanie DeLuca, Benny Goldman, Matthew Jackson, Larry Katz, Theresa Kuchler, Michael Stepner, and Johannes Stroebel – in a team-oriented lab environment, with regular lab meetings, seminars, and other events. Fellows also have the opportunity to support our research translation and policy work through such resources as the Opportunity Atlas, the Social Capital Atlas, and the Economic Tracker. Fellows are invited to participate in broader activities at Harvard and Brown, including seminars and courses. The program serves as an ideal bridge between college and graduate school for students interested in empirical economics. Most previous fellows have gone on to top Ph.D. programs. job_a83fce4e2bd8ea24: About the Opportunity Job Summary Northeastern University’s Coastal Sustainability Institute (CSI) and The Nature Conservancy’s (TNC) Massachusetts and Global Science programs are partnering to offer a joint Postdoctoral Fellowship Opportunity in Coastal Sustainability. ​ ​ Northeastern University (NU) is a global leader in experiential education and research with expertise in marine and coastal ecology, environmental forecasting and climate adaptation, fisheries and ecosystem-based management, ecological engineering and restoration, environmental sociology, and sustainability science. ​ The Nature Conservancy is a world-leading conservation organization with marine priorities currently focused on sustainable fisheries, quantifying the economic benefits of coastal conservation, and the role of ecosystems in protecting societies from coastal hazards and climate change. ​ ​ NU and TNC are active partners in coastal conservation and sustainability science research and practice. As part of this ongoing partnership, NU’s CSI and TNC are excited to announce the fourth round of this Coastal Sustainability Fellows Program for postdoctoral scientists. ​ ​ The CSI-TNC Coastal Sustainability Fellows Program will foster a collaborative, intellectual environment that leverages the interdisciplinary expertise of both CSI and TNC to train postdoctoral scholars and address major challenges facing coastal communities and ecosystems. Qualifications The CSI- TNC Coastal Sustainability Fellows Program welcomes applicants from all fields of study focused on understanding and implementing solutions that promote coastal sustainability. Applicants must have earned a doctoral degree in a relevant field of natural science, social science, or engineering. The 2026 Fellowship competition will prioritize applicants with research interests related to coastal restoration, marsh migration, and community adaptation to flood risk. While not exclusive, specific areas of research connected to these priorities could include: • Addressing ecological and social barriers and enabling factors for coastal restoration, including salt marshes, oysters, and seagrasses • Understanding factors that influence land use decisions related to coastal flood risk, including floodplain protection, coastal relocation, restoration potential, and local socio-ecological dynamics • Identifying and facilitating marsh migration corridors Fellowship Details & Application Process Based on funding availability, the fellowship will provide two years of salary ($60,315 per year) and benefits plus an additional $5,000 each year to support travel for meetings and field research. Fellows will be based at NU’s CSI and Marine Science Center in Nahant, MA, and co-mentored by scientists at CSI and TNC. In addition to research, fellows will have opportunities to develop skills consistent with their goals including grant writing / fundraising, teaching, mentoring, and networking with TNC and academic partners. Initial review of applications will begin on September 21, with an anticipated start date as early as October 2026. Complete applications will include a CV, 2-4 representative publications, names and contact information for 2-3 individuals who can provide letters of recommendation, a 1-page broader impacts statement, and a 2-page research statement that identifies an academic mentor (or mentors) at CSI, and how their research will also link to TNC mentors in the Massachusetts Ocean and Climate programs. Prospective candidates should contact Alison Bowden at TNC and their potential academic mentor at CSI before applying. We are committed to promoting diversity in conservation and sustainability science and therefore strongly encourage applicants from all historically marginalized groups. The duration of this position is contingent upon the continued availability of funding from this award at its current financial level. The Research Fellow in Domestic Labor History will conduct original primary-source research to provide evidence for the Museum to document and interpret the domestic conditions that afforded Emily Dickinson the opportunity to compose a large body of poetic and epistolary work. Working with archival, manuscript, and material culture collections, the Fellow will examine records including correspondence, financial documents, census data, maps, employment records, newspapers, church records, artifacts, landscapes, the built environment, and other contemporaneous sources to identify and reconstruct the lives and labor of individual domestic workers associated with Dickinson family households and comparable homes in the region. The Fellow will investigate and analyze the social, economic, and cultural structures of nineteenth-century Amherst and New England—including systems of race, gender, class, ethnicity, immigration, and labor—that shaped the experiences, opportunities, and constraints of domestic workers. This work will situate individual biographies within broader regional contexts of domestic service, wage labor, household economies, and shifting social hierarchies. The Fellow will assess how visible and invisible labor within the home—including cooking, cleaning, laundry, caregiving, agricultural labor, animal husbandry, and other forms of household and homestead management—contributed to sustaining social, psychic, and material environments in which employers could pursue intellectual, professional, civic, and creative endeavors. The position requires critical attention to gaps and silences in the historical record and interpretive possibilities for representing individuals whose lives were often minimally documented. The Fellow will produce well-documented research findings and will work with the Senior Director of Programs to develop an interpretive framework from these findings. The Museum may incorporate research results into the visitor experience through interpretation, public programs, exhibitions, publications, and institutional scholarship, thereby advancing a fuller and more inclusive account of the historical conditions that supported Dickinson’s authorship. This position advances the institution’s commitment to inclusive, evidence-based scholarship and to expanding historical interpretation to more fully represent the lives and labor of individuals whose contributions have been understudied or marginalized in the historical record. job_e494a15351cdccfe: Job Description Summary Organization's Summary Statement: Human beings share a capacity for language, unique to the species. This capacity guides the learning of language in children and constrains the character of the languages we come to have. To study it we pursue various sources of evidence. Among them are the grammars of individual languages; patterns of grammatical variation across languages; the development, normal and abnormal, of language in children; the mental processing of language in use; and the embodiment of language in the brain. But all these perspectives converge on a single natural object: the human language faculty, whose study unifies the work at Maryland Linguistics. The Department of Linguistics at the University of Maryland combines current theoretical research in phonology, syntax, and semantics with state-of-the-art experimental research in language acquisition, computational linguistics, psycholinguistics and neurolinguistics, in order to understand the human capacity for language. Connections between our core competencies are strong, with theoretical, experimental and computational work typically pursued in tandem. A network of collaboration at all levels sustains a research climate that is both vigorous and friendly. Here new ideas develop in conversation, stimulated by the steady activity of our labs and research groups, frequent student meetings with faculty, regular talks by local and invited scholars and collaborations with a campus community of over 200 language scientists. job_fe32a9e5a070f101: Position Title: Assistant Professor in Applied Linguistics and Artificial Intelligence (AI) Appointment Type: Faculty Job Description: Summary of Duties and Responsibilities: The Department of English in the College of Liberal Arts and Sciences at Iowa State University in Ames, Iowa invites applications for a tenure-track Assistant Professor in Applied Linguistics and Artificial Intelligence (AI). This faculty member will strengthen cross-disciplinary efforts in an area of excellence in the Department of English—the use of technology for teaching, assessing, and researching language.
